articles.title: Congo arrests hundreds of Chinese miners in copper heartland - Mining.com
articles.summary: Congo arrests hundreds of Chinese miners in copper heartland  Mining.comDR Congo Detains Around 300 Chinese Nationals in Mining Crackdown  MiningMXThe Digital Webinar Series: DRC’s 2027 Critical Minerals & Industrialisation Forum  Mining Review Africa
articles.full_text:
About 300 Chinese nationals working in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s copper belt were detained earlier this week as part of a crackdown on illegal mining, according to people familiar with the matter.
The arrests took place mostly in the mining hub of Kolwezi, the people said, asking not to be named describing a sensitive issue. Chinese companies dominate copper output in Congo, and workers were arrested for their alleged involvement in illicit mining on concessions belonging to other firms, according to some of the people.
The officials carrying out the arrests included agents from Congo’s National Security Council and immigration authority, some of the people said. The Chinese embassy in Kinshasa intervened and some of the workers have since been released, they said.
The Chinese embassy, and Congo’s mining ministry, immigration authority and presidency didn’t respond to requests for comment.
A wave of mainly Chinese investment has fueled Congo’s copper expansion in recent years, helping the nation triple output since 2015 and surpass Peru as the world’s second-largest producer. But the mining boom has also brought disorder.
Artisanal miners, sometimes supported by soldiers, have repeatedly operated without authorization on permits held by international investors.
(By William Clowes and Julian Luk)

articles.title: Nigeria, World Bank Move to Tackle AfCFTA Digital Trade Barriers - Nigeria Communications Week
articles.summary: Nigeria, World Bank Move to Tackle AfCFTA Digital Trade Barriers  Nigeria Communications Week
articles.full_text:
Nigeria is working with the World Bank Group to identify regulatory gaps affecting digital trade as the country seeks to align its domestic policies with the African Continental Free Trade Area’s Digital Trade Protocol.
According to the Nigerian AfCFTA Coordination Office, the initiative will examine how the country’s pending digital economy legislation and planned e-commerce policy can be aligned with continental rules intended to facilitate cross-border digital commerce.
Patience Okala, the office’s national coordinator and chief executive, said the regulatory gap analysis aims to ensure that the protocol, its annexes and Nigeria’s domestic laws and policies operate consistently.
The development comes as African governments seek to reduce regulatory obstacles that prevent businesses from expanding their digital services beyond national borders.
Nigeria has identified Ghana, Egypt, Rwanda, South Africa and Kenya as priority markets for domestic businesses seeking regional expansion. Regulators from the five countries had visited Lagos to examine market-access requirements and identify areas where regulatory processes could be aligned or mutually recognised, Okala said.
Differences in national regulations can complicate cross-border e-commerce, digital payments, electronic transactions and the handling of data.
Businesses operating across multiple African markets may need to navigate different requirements for digital documentation, consumer protection, payment services and regulatory compliance. For smaller companies, these differences can increase the cost of entering new markets and make it harder to scale services across the continent.
In an August 2026 report, the World Bank argued that Africa’s next phase of economic integration depends on reducing trade and regulatory friction and improving connections between national systems. The report identified digital networks, payment infrastructure, customs procedures and services as important components of a more integrated regional market.
The AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol provides a continental framework for addressing some of these challenges. Its implementation, however, depends on countries translating regional commitments into domestic laws, regulations and operational systems.
Nigeria’s proposed National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill is part of that process. The legislation is intended to establish a broader legal framework for the country’s digital economy, while the planned e-commerce policy is expected to support the development of online commercial activity.
The regulatory review will help identify where existing rules and proposed measures need to be aligned with the continental framework.
In related news, Nigeria has also been selected as one of three pilot countries for the Africa Digital Access and Public Infrastructure for Trade initiative, alongside Egypt and Kenya.
The programme, run by the AfCFTA Secretariat and the Tony Blair Institute, aims to advance interoperability between digital systems and support implementation of the Digital Trade Protocol. A team has been inaugurated in Nigeria to work on the initiative, according to Okala.

articles.title: Tanzania Advances Southern Railway Plan with Egypt’s Arab Contractors - The Chanzo
articles.summary: Tanzania Advances Southern Railway Plan with Egypt’s Arab Contractors  The Chanzo
articles.full_text:
Dar es Salaam — Tanzania has taken a step towards developing a railway linking Mtwara Port with mineral-rich southern regions and Mbamba Bay on Lake Nyasa after Tanzania Railways Corporation (TRC) signed an agreement with Egypt’s state-owned construction company, Arab Contractors, to conduct preliminary studies and a feasibility assessment.
The proposed Southern Corridor Railway Line, estimated at approximately 1,000 kilometres, aims to facilitate the transportation of minerals, agricultural produce and industrial goods while improving access to regional markets. A branch is also planned to serve the Mchuchuma coal and Liganga iron ore projects.
Speaking during the signing ceremony, Friday, October 16, 2026, TRC Director General Machibya Shiwa said the agreement establishes a framework for technical and financial studies, including an assessment of possible financing options for the project.
“Under the agreement, Arab Contractors will undertake preliminary studies at its own cost and is expected to submit an initial report within three months,” said Machibya, “TRC will provide technical information, coordinate relevant institutions and review the findings.”
Transport Minister Professor Makame Mbarawa said the railway could unlock economic opportunities in southern Tanzania by connecting agricultural production areas, mineral deposits and industrial projects with Mtwara Port.
READ MORE: Tanzania, Burundi Kick Off Landmark Standard Gauge Railway Project
He directed both parties to establish a work plan defining responsibilities, expected results and implementation timelines. He also stressed that the studies must examine actual freight demand, construction costs, financing options and the long-term sustainability of railway operations.
“The agreements being signed today constitute a preparatory step for this important project,” Mbarawa said, adding that the studies should establish transport requirements, economic benefits and possible financing arrangements.
Reviving the Mtwara Development Corridor
The proposal also revives ambitions associated with the Mtwara Development Corridor, a regional initiative advanced by Southern African Development Community (SADC) leaders in 2004 to promote trade and investment among Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique and Zambia.
The initiative envisaged coordinated infrastructure development, including roads, railways, ports, bridges, energy networks and telecommunications, to connect previously underserved areas with regional and international markets.
Proposed projects included the Unity Bridge across the Ruvuma River between Tanzania and Mozambique, improved transport infrastructure connections between Mtwara and Mbamba Bay, and transport links across Lake Nyasa. Energy cooperation and the development of Mchuchuma’s coal reserves were also identified as potential drivers of regional growth.
READ MORE: AfDB Approves Over $600m for 650-Kilometre Tanzania, Burundi Rail Infrastructure
More than two decades later, the Southern Corridor Railway could help realise part of that vision. Yet its regional benefits will depend on complementary investments and cooperation with neighbouring countries.
A connection to Mbamba Bay could facilitate onward transportation towards Malawi and Mozambique, while Mtwara Port could offer regional businesses another gateway to international markets.
Building on railway expansion
The proposed southern line would complement Tanzania’s broader railway development programme, including the Standard Gauge Railway network connecting central Tanzania with destinations such as Mwanza and Kigoma.
While those investments strengthen transport along the country’s central axis, the Southern Corridor Railway would focus on connecting southern production centres with the coast and neighbouring markets.
Arab Contractors brings experience from major infrastructure projects in Tanzania, having participated in the consortium involved in implementing the 2,115-megawatt Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project. However, its current agreement concerns feasibility studies and does not constitute a construction contract.
Beyond minerals, improved railway access could support agricultural trade, industrial investment, employment and tourism. The corridor encompasses attractions including Lake Nyasa, the Kitulo Plateau, Selous Game Reserve, Indian Ocean beaches and marine parks.
Nevertheless, these benefits will require complementary investment, local skills development, environmental protection and meaningful community participation.

articles.title: Railway tracks return to Arish after decades as Sinai rail project advances - Urban & Transport - Egypt - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Railway tracks return to Arish after decades as Sinai rail project advances - Urban & Transport - Egypt  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
Railway tracks have reached Arish for the first time since 1967, local media reported, marking a long-awaited step toward reconnecting the North Sinai city to Egypt’s national railway network.
The arrival advances the Sinai railway project, a roughly 500-kilometre route linking Fardan, East Port Said, Bir Al-Abd, Arish and Taba to serve passengers, industry and trade across the peninsula.
Sinai News Network published footage late Friday, credited to journalist Ahmed Abu Deraa, showing rails laid on concrete sleepers and describing their arrival as the first since 1967.
The footage drew celebratory reactions on social media, with users welcoming the railway’s return and expressing pride in development efforts across Sinai.
The construction marks a new chapter for Arish, where the railway once carried passengers and goods across northern Sinai before the June 1967 war cut its connection to Egypt’s national network.
In a September statement, the Ministry of Transport said 11 Egyptian companies were carrying out earthworks on the 83-kilometer Bir Al-Abd–Arish section, along with the construction of seven stations.
These include Al-Sadat, Al-Teloul, Shuhadaa Al-Rawda, Salt Factory, Al-Masaeed, Sinai–Central Arish, and Arish Airport, serving villages, residential communities, industrial facilities, and the airport.
The project includes separate 12-kilometre railway connections to Arish Port and a cement factory. The port connection complements the Arish Port expansion, enabling goods to move between the Mediterranean gateway and the national railway network.
Engineering works include nine crossing bridges, a railway alignment bridge and two tunnels. The ministry said Transport Minister Kamel Al-Wazir also directed the construction of an underpass at Al-Mazar village to facilitate residents’ movement.
Further sections extend 85 kilometres from Arish to Al-Hasana and 173 kilometres from Al-Hasana to Taba.
Al-Wazir described the railway as a development corridor, transporting people and goods and supporting economic activity across Sinai.
The railway is a central component of the Arish–Taba logistics corridor, linking the Mediterranean with the Gulf of Aqaba through industrial and mining areas in central Sinai. According to the ministry, it will connect factories and production centres to domestic markets and export routes via the ports of Arish and Taba.
Egypt began passenger railway trials on the 100-kilometre Fardan–Bir Al-Abd section on 7 October 2024.
Egyptian National Railways operates four daily passenger journeys between Qantara East and Bir Al-Abd using upgraded Tahya Misr coaches. The service covers eight stations, providing a transport link for communities along the route.
The railway accompanies broader investment in the peninsula. Egypt allocated around EGP 35 billion for Sinai development across the 2025/2026 and 2026/2027 fiscal years.
Arish’s railway history dates to January 1917, when the British military railway being built across Sinai reached the city before extending to Rafah that March, according to Sinai heritage researcher Mahmoud Al-Shorbagy. The line subsequently carried civilian passengers and goods.
An earlier restoration project opened the Fardan–Bir Al-Abd railway in 2001 but stopped short of Arish. The current extension aims to complete that connection before continuing south toward Taba.

articles.title: South Africa remains Africa’s largest economy at $489.1 billion in latest rankings, but sluggish growth and high unemployment cloud its dominance - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: South Africa remains Africa’s largest economy at $489.1 billion in latest rankings, but sluggish growth and high unemployment cloud its dominance  Business Insider AfricaKenya overtakes Ethiopia as East Africa’s largest economy after five years of trailing  Business DailyEthiopia loses East Africa's largest economy title to Kenya, falling $24 billion behind in latest rankings  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Despite its economic size, the country faces slow growth, weak investment, and persistent infrastructure challenges.
- Public debt is projected to reach 78.5% of GDP, further limiting fiscal flexibility and growth prospects.
- Government reforms target electricity and logistics, but greater investment, job creation, and infrastructure upgrades are needed for sustained competitiveness.
Figures from the IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook place South Africa ahead of Egypt, Nigeria and Algeria, reaffirming its position as the continent’s largest economy by nominal GDP.
Egypt ranks second with $442.89 billion, followed by Nigeria at $386.67 billion and Algeria at $331.89 billion. Morocco completes the top five with $195.63 billion.
South Africa’s economy is $46.19 billion larger than Egypt’s and $102.41 billion ahead of Nigeria’s.
The country's position reflects its established financial services, mining, manufacturing and retail sectors.
However, its economic strength has not translated into faster growth or sufficient employment opportunities.
Slow growth weighs on economic performance
South Africa continues to record modest growth compared with several other major African economies, constrained by weak domestic demand, infrastructure challenges and subdued private investment.
The IMF projected economic growth of 1.4% in 2026, below the rates expected in Ethiopia, Uganda and Tanzania.
Statistics South Africa reported that the economy contracted by 0.2% in the second quarter of 2026, reversing the 0.4% growth recorded in the preceding quarter.
Mining, manufacturing and trade contributed to the decline, while freight rail inefficiencies, port congestion and infrastructure constraints continued to affect businesses.
Unemployment remains stubbornly high
South Africa's unemployment rate increased to 33.6% in the second quarter of 2026, up from 32.7% in the previous quarter, according to Statistics South Africa.
The number of unemployed people rose by 345,000 to 8.5 million, while employment declined by 16,000 to 16.7 million.
Youth unemployment remains particularly severe, reflecting limited job opportunities, skills mismatches and weak economic growth.
The labour market challenges have continued to weigh on household incomes and consumer spending, reinforcing concerns about the country's ability to convert economic output into broader prosperity.
Investment and debt pressures persist
South Africa also faces challenges attracting sufficient investment to support faster economic expansion.
An October 2026 Financial Times report indicated that only about half of the R1.5 trillion in investment pledges secured since 2018 had materialised, while fixed investment had declined in four of the previous six quarters.
Public debt remains another concern. The IMF's February 2026 assessment projected government debt at 78.5% of GDP in 2026, limiting fiscal flexibility.
President Cyril Ramaphosa's administration has pursued electricity and logistics reforms to improve business conditions and encourage private sector investment.
Despite these efforts, South Africa continues to face pressure to accelerate growth and employment creation as other African economies expand more rapidly.
While its financial system and industrial base continue to underpin its economic leadership, sustained investment, infrastructure improvements and job creation remain essential to maintaining its competitiveness.

articles.title: African Business Council re-elects Amani Asfour for second term, puts AfCFTA implementation in focus - Daily News Egypt
articles.summary: African Business Council re-elects Amani Asfour for second term, puts AfCFTA implementation in focus  Daily News Egypt
articles.full_text:
The African Business Council (AfBC) has re-elected Amani Asfour as its president for a second term, reaffirming the confidence of African private-sector leaders in her vision to strengthen continental economic integration, boost intra-African trade and investment, and accelerate industrial development.
The re-election took place during the council’s General Assembly meeting in El Alamein, held alongside the African Private Sector High-Level Forum, the African Union’s Mid-Year Coordination Summit and the El Alamein African Business Summit.
The General Assembly also elected four vice presidents representing regional and sectoral private-sector institutions across the continent. They are James Chimwaza, former president of the COMESA Business Council; Mijgan Kazmir, vice president of the Federation of West African Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FEWACCI); Charles Kahuthu, CEO of the East African Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture; and Mansour Ahmed, president of the Pan African Manufacturers Association (PAMA).
The newly elected leadership is expected to strengthen the council’s continental representation and advocacy for policies supporting business competitiveness, regional integration, industrial development and cross-border investment.
Speaking after her re-election, Asfour said the council would continue working towards a more competitive and innovative Africa, with the private sector playing a central role in the continent’s economic transformation.
She described the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as a historic opportunity to unlock Africa’s economic potential, stressing the need to accelerate intra-African trade, strengthen regional value chains, promote industrialisation, and support small and medium-sized enterprises, women entrepreneurs and young business leaders.
Asfour also called for a shift away from reliance on raw material exports towards producing higher-value goods manufactured in Africa, highlighting the importance of quality standards, competitiveness and value addition.
“Together, we will continue working towards our vision: One Africa, One Market, One Prosperous Future,” she said.
Established under a decision by the African Union’s Assembly of Heads of State and Government, the AfBC serves as a continental platform representing businesses of different sizes, including large companies, small and medium-sized enterprises, women-led businesses and youth-led ventures.
The council works to strengthen private-sector participation in policymaking, facilitate trade, encourage investment partnerships and improve the business environment across African markets.
During its new term, the council plans to deepen cooperation with the African Union Commission, the AfCFTA Secretariat, regional economic communities, chambers of commerce, manufacturers’ associations and development partners.
Its priorities include removing barriers to intra-African trade, mobilising investment, developing regional industrial value chains and expanding economic opportunities for small businesses, women and young people, in support of the African Union’s Agenda 2063 and its vision of a prosperous and integrated continent.

articles.title: African mineral powerhouse DR Congo bars contact with former colonial ruler over raids on president’s family members - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: African mineral powerhouse DR Congo bars contact with former colonial ruler over raids on president’s family members  Business Insider AfricaBelgian police search homes of relatives of Congo's Tshisekedi  ReutersFormer colonial power Belgium launches raids on President Tshisekedi’s family over DRC mining money laundering  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Belgian police raided properties linked to relatives and associates of DRC President Félix Tshisekedi as part of a money-laundering investigation tied to mining revenues.
- In response, the DRC ordered its presidential cabinet to halt all direct and indirect contact with the Belgian embassy and its staff.
- The investigation centers on alleged misappropriation and laundering of mining revenues, following complaints by Congolese NGOs and former Gécamines directors.
- Nine associates and relatives of Tshisekedi, reportedly Belgian nationals, are under investigation, but there is no evidence implicating Tshisekedi himself.
Belgium’s police raids on properties linked to relatives and associates of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Félix Tshisekedi have triggered diplomatic tensions, with Kinshasa ordering its presidential cabinet to suspend contact with the Belgian embassy.
Read Also
The directive comes amid a money-laundering investigation linked to the alleged misappropriation of mining revenues in the DRC, a country rich in copper, cobalt, gold and other minerals critical to global industries.
The move adds strain to relations between the central African nation and its former colonial ruler, although the Congolese presidency has not officially confirmed that the restriction is a response to the Belgian investigation.
Anadolu Agency reports that the directive signed by presidential chief of staff Anthony Nkinzo Kamole instructs members of the presidential cabinet to avoid direct or indirect contact with the Belgian embassy and its diplomatic and administrative staff until further notice.
“All members of the Office of the President of the Republic, in the exercise of their duties, are requested to refrain, until further notice, from any direct or indirect contact” with the embassy as well as with its diplomatic and administrative staff, the circular reads in part.
Any necessary communication must be authorised and channelled through the DRC’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, according to reports on the circular.
Probe centres on alleged mining revenue laundering
The searches were conducted on October 14 in Brussels and surrounding areas as part of an investigation launched after complaints filed in 2025 by Congolese non-governmental organisations and former directors of state-owned mining company Gécamines.
Belgian lawyer Bernard Maingain and France-based Congolese lawyer Hervé Diakese, who represent the complainants, said the case concerns the alleged misappropriation of mining revenues and resources belonging to local communities, as well as the laundering of proceeds.
Diakese said the alleged activities deprived Congolese communities and the state of resources while allowing those involved to maintain lifestyles beyond what their legitimate incomes would support.
Media reports say nine relatives and associates of Tshisekedi, all reportedly Belgian nationals, are under investigation over alleged involvement in the plundering of mines in the mineral-rich provinces of Haut-Katanga and Lualaba. Belgian prosecutors have not publicly identified those targeted by the searches.
The allegations have not been proven in court, and no official evidence has established that Tshisekedi himself is implicated in the investigation.
The restriction on embassy contact applies to the presidential cabinet and does not amount to a formal severance of diplomatic relations between Kinshasa and Brussels.

articles.title: Envoy charges Nigeria, Ghana to demolish trade barriers, build joint industries - The Sun Nigeria
articles.summary: Envoy charges Nigeria, Ghana to demolish trade barriers, build joint industries  The Sun Nigeria
articles.full_text:
Nigeria and Ghana have been urged to dismantle trade barriers, improve cross-border investment and build joint industries to unlock the full potential of their economic relationship and strengthen regional integration.
Nigeria’s High Commissioner to Ghana, Ambassador Olufemi Abikoye, made the call while delivering a keynote address at the 2026 Nigeria Union of Traders Association, Ghana (NUTAG) Award Night on Saturday, October 10.
Abikoye said the two West African countries must move beyond historical friendship and ordinary trade towards a deliberate economic partnership built on shared production, stronger value chains and measurable business outcomes.
He argued that although Nigeria and Ghana had maintained longstanding economic, political and cultural ties, history alone could not guarantee prosperity without practical policies to facilitate trade and investment.
According to him, the two countries should shift from viewing each other primarily as competing markets to recognising the opportunities for cooperation in manufacturing, agriculture, finance, infrastructure and technology.
“Nigeria and Ghana are not simply two countries that happen to occupy the same region. We are two principal economic, political and cultural anchors of West Africa,” he said.
He noted that their peoples had traded, studied, worked and lived across borders for generations, adding that the existing relationship needed to be formalised, expanded and modernised to deliver greater economic benefits.
The envoy identified the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as a major opportunity for the countries to deepen economic cooperation and expand their reach across the continent.
He noted that Nigeria assumed the chairmanship of the AfCFTA Council of Ministers Bureau in July 2026, creating an opportunity to advance implementation and secure tangible benefits for African businesses.
According to him, Nigeria’s large market and economic scale, combined with Ghana’s strategic location, commercial infrastructure and role as host of the AfCFTA Secretariat, could help both countries develop products for the wider African market.
“Together, our economies can do much more than simply sell finished products to one another. We can produce together for Africa,” he said.
Abikoye also cautioned against protectionism, saying investments by companies from either country should be assessed by the value they create rather than perceived as threats to local businesses.
He said cross-border investments could generate employment, transfer technology, strengthen local supply chains, increase tax revenue and improve foreign exchange earnings.
He urged both governments to create a predictable and transparent business environment that would give investors confidence to operate across borders.
The envoy further called for a shift from exporting raw commodities to processing them locally, manufacturing finished products and developing African brands capable of competing in international markets.
He identified agriculture, cocoa, cashew, oil and minerals as areas where Nigerian and Ghanaian businesses could collaborate to retain more economic value within the continent.
Rather than exporting commodities and allowing other countries to capture much of the value through processing and manufacturing, he said, businesses should work together to develop production networks, logistics systems and higher-value products.
Abikoye cited the recent onion trade dispute between Nigeria and Ghana as an example of how commercial disagreements could strain relations and disrupt supplies.
He said the experience underscored the need for effective mechanisms to resolve trade disputes before they escalated into diplomatic tensions.
To address the challenges, he proposed a practical Nigeria-Ghana Business Compact built around five commitments: predictable market access, faster dispute resolution, easier movement of people and services, increased cross-border investment, and the development of regional value chains.
Under the proposal, both governments would identify and remove unnecessary non-tariff barriers, overlapping regulations, arbitrary restrictions and avoidable delays at border crossings.
He also advocated reliable channels for commercial mediation, arbitration and regulatory engagement to ensure that disagreements between businesses did not become disputes between the two countries.
On the movement of people, he said regional integration should cover not only goods but also professionals, including engineers, bankers, consultants, lawyers and entrepreneurs whose expertise could support business growth.
He urged pension funds, banks, private equity firms, development-finance institutions and corporate investors in both countries to explore investment opportunities in each other’s markets.
Abikoye said the ultimate objective should be to enable Nigerian and Ghanaian businesses to jointly produce goods and services for Africa and the global market, without being hindered by unnecessary bureaucratic obstacles.
He concluded that the two countries had the history, business relationships and continental framework needed to build a stronger economic partnership, but stressed that implementation was now critical.
He called on governments and the private sector to translate declarations of friendship into practical commercial results, including making it easier for goods produced in Nigerian cities such as Aba to reach Ghanaian markets and for products from Ghana’s Tema to be sold in Nigerian cities such as Kano.
“Now is the time to go far together,” he said, urging both countries to make the celebration a starting point for a new era of business cooperation.

articles.title: Tanzania Revives 1,000km Mtwara Railway Plan - Uchumi360
articles.summary: Tanzania Revives 1,000km Mtwara Railway Plan  Uchumi360
articles.full_text:
Ready
Tanzania has signed a new agreement with Egypt’s Arab Contractors to reassess the proposed 1,000 kilometre railway linking Mtwara, Songea, Mbamba Bay, Mchuchuma and Liganga. The project has already undergone earlier feasibility work, making freight demand, industrial development and financing the central questions behind its latest revival.
Tanzania has reopened one of its most ambitious southern infrastructure plans after Tanzania Railways Corporation signed a memorandum of understanding with Egypt’s Arab Contractors on October 16, 2026, covering new technical and financial work for the proposed standard gauge railway connecting Mtwara Port with Songea, Mbamba Bay and branches towards the Mchuchuma coal and Liganga iron ore projects. The proposed network, repeatedly described by government as approximately 1,000 kilometres, would create an east to west transport corridor across southern Tanzania, connecting the Indian Ocean with Lake Nyasa while providing heavy freight infrastructure for some of the country’s largest undeveloped mineral and industrial projects. Arab Contractors will undertake the preliminary work at its own cost and is expected to submit an initial report within three months, according to TRC Director General Machibya Shiwa, while Transport Minister Professor Makame Mbarawa has described the agreement as “a preparatory step” and said the work must determine actual transport demand, construction costs, economic benefits and possible financing arrangements before Tanzania proceeds further.
The distinction between preparing the project and beginning construction is important because the Mtwara to Mbamba Bay railway is not a new idea and Tanzania is not studying the route for the first time. Government has previously told Parliament that feasibility and preliminary design work had already been completed, while an earlier feasibility study dating to around 2016 was subsequently identified as requiring review before the project could be taken to investors. By 2024, government had allocated funding for a transaction adviser to help update the project, prepare procurement documentation and examine implementation through a public private partnership, and by early 2026 officials were still describing the railway as a project whose feasibility work had been completed but whose financing remained unresolved. The new Arab Contractors assignment should therefore be understood less as a first investigation into whether a railway can physically be built across southern Tanzania and more as an attempt to establish whether the economics of the corridor have changed sufficiently for the project to become financeable.
That question has become more relevant because several of the projects that were always supposed to provide the railway with its economic purpose are moving back onto the government’s active development agenda. The Mchuchuma coal and Liganga iron and steel projects have spent years moving between negotiation, redesign and delay, leaving the proposed railway without the large and predictable freight volumes that normally justify heavy rail infrastructure. In 2026, however, government again signalled an intention to move the projects into implementation from 2027, while work is also progressing at Mbamba Bay Port and Mtwara continues to be positioned as a southern maritime gateway. The railway is therefore being reconsidered at a moment when the industrial geography around it may be becoming materially different from the one that existed when the earlier feasibility study was undertaken a decade ago.
The Railway Will Ultimately Be Decided by Freight
The strongest economic case for the Mtwara to Mbamba Bay railway has never been passenger transport. It is the movement of heavy commodities and industrial cargo over long distances at costs that road transport cannot easily match. Mchuchuma contains approximately 428 million tonnes of identified coal reserves, while earlier development plans contemplated production of around three million tonnes of coal annually alongside a 600 MW power station. Liganga contains roughly 126 million tonnes of identified iron ore reserves in the explored area and has historically been designed around large scale iron and steel production, with plans that have ranged from around one million tonnes of steel annually to considerably higher output under later government proposals. If those projects begin producing at scale, the logistics problem becomes immediately obvious: millions of tonnes of coal, ore, steel, machinery and industrial inputs cannot be moved efficiently for hundreds of kilometres by relying predominantly on trucks without imposing high transport costs, road maintenance burdens and congestion.
This is why Mbarawa’s insistence that the new work establish real transport demand should be regarded as the central economic issue behind the agreement. A railway of this scale carries very high fixed costs regardless of how many trains eventually run over it. Track, bridges, signalling, rolling stock, stations, maintenance facilities and associated infrastructure must all be financed before the first tonne of freight generates revenue. The commercial question is therefore not whether southern Tanzania possesses enough resources to make the map attractive, but whether those resources can produce reliable annual cargo volumes large enough to support the capital cost of the railway. For financiers, three million tonnes of committed coal production is much more useful than a geological reserve of hundreds of millions of tonnes that may remain underground, just as an operating steel complex provides a stronger revenue case than a proposed factory whose development timetable remains uncertain.
That relationship also works in reverse, which is one reason the corridor has been difficult to unlock. Mining and industrial investors want confidence that their products can reach markets at competitive transport costs before committing billions of dollars to production, while railway investors want confidence that the mines and factories will exist before financing the infrastructure designed to serve them. Tanzania therefore faces a coordination problem rather than a simple construction problem. Mchuchuma, Liganga, Mtwara Port, Mbamba Bay and the railway become substantially more valuable when developed as parts of one industrial system, but each project becomes harder to finance when the others remain uncertain. The importance of the latest study will depend on whether it can connect those projects through credible production schedules, freight commitments and financing structures rather than simply updating engineering drawings.
Mtwara and Mbamba Bay Could Create a New Southern Trade Axis
At the eastern end of the proposed corridor sits Mtwara Port, whose long term strategic potential has always been larger than its current hinterland. Tanzania has invested in the port partly because southern Tanzania possesses significant natural gas, agricultural and mineral resources, but maritime infrastructure can only attract large volumes when inland transport makes it economical for producers and traders to reach the coast. Dar es Salaam has historically dominated Tanzanian international trade because it is connected to the country’s principal road and rail networks and to important inland markets in Tanzania and neighbouring states. Mtwara has never enjoyed the same concentration of transport infrastructure, limiting the size of the commercial territory from which it can realistically draw cargo.
A railway extending through Songea and towards Mbamba Bay would materially change that calculation. Coal, iron ore, steel, agricultural produce and manufactured goods could move towards the Indian Ocean at lower unit costs, while imported machinery, equipment, fuel and industrial inputs could travel inland. The railway would therefore expand the effective economic hinterland of Mtwara Port rather than simply provide another transport option between existing towns. If the industrial projects along the route develop as planned, the port could increasingly function as the maritime end of a dedicated southern production corridor rather than as an infrastructure asset waiting for sufficient inland cargo to emerge.

articles.title: Ethiopia loses East Africa's largest economy title to Kenya, falling $24 billion behind in latest rankings - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Ethiopia loses East Africa's largest economy title to Kenya, falling $24 billion behind in latest rankings  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Kenya has overtaken Ethiopia as East Africa's largest economy, mainly due to the depreciation of the Ethiopian birr.
- Kenya's GDP is projected at $135.92 billion in 2025, ahead of Ethiopia's $126.35 billion, with the gap expected to widen to $24 billion in 2026.
- Renewed insecurity in Ethiopia's Tigray region and concerns over the 2022 peace agreement could further deter foreign investment and harm economic stability.
- While Ethiopia maintains stronger real GDP growth rates than Kenya, currency movements and investor preferences have shifted economic leadership in the region back to Kenya.
According to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) October 2026 World Economic Outlook, Kenya’s gross domestic product (GDP) stood at $135.92 billion in 2025, surpassing Ethiopia’s $126.35 billion by $9.57 billion.
The shift marks a significant reversal in East Africa's economic rankings, with Kenya reclaiming its position as the region's largest economy after roughly five years.
The gap is projected to widen to $24 billion in 2026, strengthening Kenya's standing as a regional commercial hub while Ethiopia faces currency pressures and renewed security concerns that could undermine investor confidence.
Kenya reclaims East Africa's economic lead
Ethiopia's economy, valued at $210 billion in 2024, fell to $126.35 billion in dollar terms in 2025 following major currency reforms.
In July 2024, the country introduced a more market-determined exchange-rate system under an IMF-supported $3.4 billion financing programme, allowing the birr to depreciate against the US dollar.
Consequently, Ethiopia's economic output lost substantial value when converted into dollars, despite continued growth in domestic production.
Kenya, meanwhile, benefited from a relatively stable shilling, which helped preserve the dollar value of its economy.
Currency movements largely explain the reversal in rankings rather than a significant difference in the countries' underlying economic growth.
However, Ethiopia still has a larger economy than Kenya when measured by purchasing power parity (PPP), which accounts for differences in local prices. Kenya's lead is based on nominal GDP measured in US dollars.
Tigray conflict adds to Ethiopia's investment challenges
While currency depreciation has reshaped the economic rankings, Ethiopia also faces renewed security challenges that could affect its investment prospects.
Fresh fighting between federal forces and Tigrayan rebels has raised concerns about the country's stability and economic recovery.
On October 16, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced a caretaker administration for Tigray after government-aligned forces regained control of the regional capital, Mekelle.
The developments have raised concerns about the durability of the 2022 peace agreement, while tensions with neighbouring Eritrea have heightened fears of wider regional instability.
The insecurity could discourage foreign investment, disrupt trade and increase operating costs, particularly for companies planning long-term infrastructure and manufacturing projects.
The IMF has also identified domestic security risks as a potential threat to Ethiopia's economic outlook.
Meanwhile, Kenya could attract investors seeking alternative regional business locations, supported by Nairobi's established financial services, technology and logistics sectors.
The country's investment ambitions are reflected in Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote's proposed $16 billion oil refinery in Lamu, a project that could strengthen Kenya's position as an industrial and energy hub if completed.
However, Kenya continues to face economic challenges, including high public debt, borrowing costs and pressure on government finances.
Ethiopia maintains stronger economic growth despite losing top position
Despite falling behind Kenya in nominal GDP, Ethiopia continues to record stronger underlying economic growth.
IMF estimates show Ethiopia's economy expanded by 9.2% in real terms in 2025, compared with Kenya's 4.6%, demonstrating that the change in rankings largely reflects exchange-rate movements rather than faster growth in Kenyan production.
Looking ahead, the IMF projects Kenya's GDP will reach $151.15 billion in 2026, compared with Ethiopia's $127.15 billion, widening the gap between the two economies to $24 billion.
The projections also place Kenya seventh among Africa's largest economies, behind South Africa, Egypt, Nigeria, Algeria, Morocco and Angola.

Malaysia’s Envoy on Diplomatic Momentum, Transformation, and Shared Futures
As Malaysia and Ethiopia celebrate 60 years of diplomatic relations, the recent reopening of the Malaysian Embassy in Addis Ababa marks a renewed chapter in bilateral engagement. Rooted in shared ambitions for growth and cooperation, the partnership between the two nations bridges Southeast Asia and the Horn of Africa at a time when both countries are actively redefining their roles on the global stage. While Malaysia has transformed from an agrarian economy into an export-oriented industrial and technological powerhouse—offering valuable structural lessons for Ethiopia’s ongoing economic reforms—trade between the two nations continues to hold untapped potential.
In this exclusive interview with The Reporter, Sara Solomon has sat down with Mohd Afandi bin Abu Bakar, Chargé d’Affaires of the Embassy of Malaysia. With nearly two decades of diplomatic experience spanning the Middle East, North America, and Southeast Asia, Mr. Mohd Afandi discusses how cultural diplomacy, strategic agro-processing partnerships, and industrial park optimization can elevate bilateral ties. Reflecting on Malaysia’s journey, he highlights how development and heritage can coexist, noting that “development and heritage preservation do not have to be competing priorities.”
Touching on the broader geopolitical landscape—including Malaysia joining the BRICS framework as a Partner Country alongside Ethiopia’s full membership—the Chargé d’Affaires elaborates on how South-South cooperation and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) can serve as catalysts for mutual prosperity. Emphasizing the transition from dialogue to action, he remarks, “The real opportunity is to build two-way commercial linkages between both countries and their stakeholders.” Excerpts:
The recent event showcasing the UNESCO-registered Malaysian Breakfast Culture paired traditional Malaysian dishes with Ethiopian ingredients. In what ways can such cultural exchanges translate into tangible economic and trade cooperation between Malaysia and Ethiopia?
I believe food is one of the most accessible and effective ways of bringing people together. When people sit around the same table, they have an opportunity not only to taste something new, but also to understand the history, traditions, and values behind it. Malaysia’s breakfast culture itself reflects this spirit. It brings together people from different ethnic and cultural backgrounds, and UNESCO recognized this living tradition in 2024 as Breakfast culture in Malaysia: dining experience in a multi-ethnic society.
From a diplomatic perspective, these cultural exchanges can create the trust and familiarity that eventually support wider bilateral relationships. A food event may begin with something as simple as nasi lemak, injera, or coffee, but the conversations that follow can open doors for tourism, hospitality, agriculture, food processing, and business partnerships. In the case of Malaysia and Ethiopia, we hope such people-to-people connections will complement our broader efforts to expand trade and investment between the two countries.
Malaysian breakfast culture was recognized as a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2024. How does Malaysia balance preserving its rich traditional heritage while aggressively pursuing rapid modern infrastructure and economic growth?
For Malaysia, development and heritage preservation do not have to be competing priorities. Our experience has shown that modernization can take place while communities continue to practice and pass on their traditions. In fact, UNESCO’s description of Malaysian breakfast culture emphasizes that the tradition has been transmitted from generation to generation and continues to bring together Malaysians of different ethnic backgrounds.
The important point is that heritage should remain a living part of society rather than simply something preserved in museums. Economic development provides new opportunities to promote traditional crafts, cuisine, music, and cultural practices, while tourism and the creative economy can provide livelihoods for communities that maintain these traditions. Malaysia’s approach is therefore about moving forward with technology and infrastructure while ensuring that our cultural identity, diversity, and traditions continue to have a meaningful place in everyday life.
Trade between our two nations has grown significantly, but there remains a notable trade imbalance heavily in Malaysia’s favor. What concrete mechanisms or incentives can be introduced to help Ethiopian exports—such as coffee, oilseeds, and livestock—gain better market access in Malaysia?
I believe the focus should be on creating more opportunities for Ethiopian products to reach Malaysian consumers and businesses, rather than looking at the trade relationship only in terms of the balance of figures. Ethiopia has strong potential in agricultural commodities, particularly coffee and other products, and Malaysia has an established market, processing industry, and distribution network. One practical area for cooperation would be to strengthen business-to-business linkages, product promotion, trade missions, and participation in specialized trade exhibitions so that Ethiopian producers can better understand Malaysian market requirements.
At the same time, market access involves more than tariffs. Standards, certification, packaging, food safety requirements, logistics, and reliable supply chains are equally important. There is scope for the relevant agencies and private-sector organizations in both countries to work together in these areas. The objective should be to help Ethiopian exporters meet Malaysian market requirements while also encouraging Malaysian importers to explore more opportunities for sourcing quality Ethiopian products.
Malaysia is a global leader in palm oil refining and agro-processing. Given Ethiopia’s massive agricultural potential, are there plans for joint ventures or technology transfers in commercial farming and food processing?
Agriculture is certainly one of the areas where I see considerable potential for stronger Malaysia–Ethiopia cooperation. Malaysia has accumulated experience not only in agricultural production, but also in downstream processing, value addition, logistics, research and development, and the development of agricultural supply chains. Ethiopia, on the other hand, has a very substantial agricultural base and a large pool of farmers and agricultural resources. There is therefore a natural basis for exploring complementarities.
Rather than looking only at the export of agricultural commodities, we should increasingly look at how value can be created locally. This could include cooperation in food processing, packaging, agricultural technology, post-harvest management, training, and commercial farming models. Whether particular joint ventures or technology-transfer projects are pursued would depend on discussions between the relevant institutions and companies, but the Embassy is certainly interested in facilitating conversations between Malaysian and Ethiopian stakeholders where there is genuine commercial potential.
Malaysia transformed from an agrarian economy into an export-oriented industrial and tech powerhouse in just a few decades. As Ethiopia undergoes key structural economic reforms, what specific lessons from Malaysia’s economic trajectory could Ethiopia adopt?
One important lesson from Malaysia’s experience is the importance of taking a long-term and consistent approach to economic transformation. Malaysia gradually moved from an economy heavily dependent on commodities toward manufacturing, services, technology, and increasingly higher-value industries. This involved investing in infrastructure and human capital, developing industrial ecosystems, attracting foreign investment, and, importantly, creating opportunities for local businesses and workers to participate in the transformation.
Malaysia mastered the setup of Industrial Parks and Free Trade Zones to attract FDI. How can Malaysian expertise assist Ethiopia in optimizing its own Industrial Parks to become regional manufacturing hubs?
Malaysia’s experience with industrial parks demonstrates that providing land and factory space alone is not sufficient to create a successful manufacturing ecosystem. Investors also look for reliable infrastructure, electricity, logistics, customs facilitation, skilled workers, access to suppliers, and clear regulatory procedures. Industrial parks work best when these elements come together and when companies can connect efficiently to both domestic and international markets.
There could therefore be useful opportunities for Malaysian institutions and companies to share experience with their Ethiopian counterparts in areas such as park management, investor facilitation, supply-chain development, skills training, and export-oriented manufacturing. Ethiopia is already undertaking reforms to improve its investment environment, including establishing special economic zones and simplifying business registration, licensing, and permit processes. Malaysia’s experience could complement these efforts, particularly where there is interest from Malaysian investors in establishing manufacturing or processing operations in Ethiopia.
Ethiopia became a full BRICS member, and Malaysia recently joined as a BRICS Partner Country, with strong endorsement from Addis Ababa. How does this shared platform reshape South-South cooperation between Southeast Asia and the Horn of Africa?

articles.title: Russian embassy highlights Egypt industrial zone, website details 2030 operating target - Urban & Transport - Egypt - Ahram Online

articles.full_text:
Russia’s embassy in Cairo highlighted on Friday the establishment of a Russian Industrial Zone in Egypt’s Suez Canal Economic Zone. It directed investors to a website outlining manufacturing opportunities, incentives, and development plans.
The embassy described the project as a special commercial and industrial complex for Russian companies in Ain Sokhna and East Port Said. Its post follows the July announcement of a selected developer.
The linked website provides detailed plans for a 50-hectare site at Ain Sokhna, with design and construction scheduled for 2026–2029 and operations targeted for 2030. It does not provide a corresponding timetable or land area for East Port Said.
Available in Russian, English, Arabic, and Chinese, the website combines a project presentation with practical guidance for prospective manufacturers. Its navigation covers advantages, infrastructure, industries, resident arrangements, and project background, along with a 14-question investor guide and inquiry forms.
The information is accompanied by port and factory imagery, maps of export destinations and SCZone facilities, and graphics explaining incentives. Historical remarks by the Egyptian and Russian presidents frame the project as a platform for industrial cooperation and exports to Africa.
Development plans and investor support
The project’s background page traces its framework to the intergovernmental agreement signed in 2018. In May 2025, SCZone and the Russian project company settled commercial terms for long-term use of the Ain Sokhna site.
The website identifies the Crystal Fund as the integrated development institution implementing the project with Russia’s Ministry of Industry and Trade. An agreement with the ministry made the fund the single point of contact for investors, developers, and future residents.
The fund’s services cover market research, project development and buyer identification; construction and utility coordination; and subsequent licensing, customs, and logistics support. The website says these services carry a fixed charge and a success fee.
It identifies Alexander Galushka as fund president, Alexander Krutikov as managing partner, and Alexander Shatunov as senior partner and head of the Egyptian project.
Manufacturers could build their own facilities on serviced plots, potentially with concessional financing, or lease premises built to their specifications. Proposed infrastructure includes electricity, gas, water, sewerage, roads, railway access and warehousing.
Manufacturing and market access
The website targets machinery, metalworking, chemicals, construction materials, transport and energy equipment, agricultural machinery, pharmaceuticals, food processing and industrial components. The background page additionally identifies petrochemicals, radio electronics, electrical equipment and timber processing.
Egypt has also sought investment from Tatarstan firms as part of its efforts to attract Russian manufacturers.
The resident guide says products could reach Egypt and overseas markets through the country’s trade agreements, subject to origin requirements and certification. The homepage advertises potential preferential access to more than 70 countries with approximately two billion consumers, while distinguishing China, India, and North America as international shipping destinations.
Residents may sell their entire output domestically, subject to applicable Egyptian taxes and customs payments. The website’s local-content references vary between at least 30 percent and more than 30 percent; eligibility for preferential exports would depend on each trade agreement.
Incentives and applications
The resident guide describes zero customs duty on eligible construction and operating imports, zero VAT on manufacturing inputs within the zone, and a three-year rent grace period.
It also outlines a deduction from net taxable profit equal to 50 percent of investment costs, subject to legal limits and capped at seven years. Elsewhere, the website calls this a corporate tax refund, leaving the precise mechanism requiring confirmation under the applicable rules.
Additional arrangements listed include full foreign ownership and renewable five-year residence permits for foreign investors.
Applicants must prepare expected products and output, building and land requirements, utility demand, imported equipment and materials, target markets, desired local content, and a proposed launch date.
The process moves from an inquiry to assessment, an individual location proposal, agreement on operating terms, and implementation support. The initial assessment creates no investment obligation, and launch timing depends on each factory’s readiness and construction requirements.
The online form requests contact and company information, sector and project details, and consent to personal data processing. The project also lists the email address rpz-egypt@crystalfund.ru and telephone number +7 (495) 129-04-44.
The zone forms part of wider Egyptian-Russian economic cooperation. Separate discussions have examined a regional grain logistics hub involving Russian exporters.
Across SCZone, Egypt inaugurated nine industrial projects worth $84.5 million in September, with nearly 2,000 jobs expected.

articles.title: Stable Decoupling: Three Tests For Europe In Face Of Chinese Economic Coercion - Analysis - Eurasia Review

articles.full_text:
By Tobias Gehrke
Key Takeaways:
- EU leaders must decide this autumn on rules for Chinese goods entering the single market, conditions for Chinese investment, and limits on Chinese suppliers in critical infrastructure, while facing a €1 billion daily trade deficit and the risk of Chinese retaliation via critical minerals.
- Drawing on the U.S. experience, the article argues that Europe can pursue targeted restrictions and stability simultaneously, using trade-defence tools, the Foreign Subsidies Regulation, and the International Procurement Instrument without allowing a narrow deal to freeze broader action.
- On investment, it calls for making more conditions mandatory under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act so Chinese projects generate local value rather than “screwdriver” assembly; on infrastructure, it urges extending high-risk supplier rules beyond 5G through the Cybersecurity Act revision.
This autumn, Europeans must decide on new terms of engagement with China. They are facing a surging EU trade deficit of €1bn a day, industrial deterioration across the continent and Chinese threats of economic coercion.
Trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic travels to Beijing this week for the final stretch of trade talks, just as Paris and Berlin publish a joint paper demanding tougher trade action against China. At a European Council summit later this month, leaders will be asked whether they wish to negotiate an agreement with China covering these issues—or whether instead to follow the Franco-German push and move to enforce European interests unilaterally by introducing tougher restrictions on China’s access to the single market.
In weighing this question, Europe’s leaders must settle three decisions: first, what rules to set for Chinese goods to enter the EU; second, what they want Chinese investment to contribute to European industry; and, third, where they should limit the roles of Chinese suppliers in critical infrastructure. Looming over all three choices is the geoeconomic reality that Beijing can retaliate—most critically, by restricting exports of critical minerals products to Europe.
The US experience
Recent US dealings with China offers guidance for how (and how not) to make such choices under threat of retaliation. In 2025, Washington assumed that imposing major tariff hikes would harm the Chinese economy and leave Beijing scrambling to make economic and political concessions. Instead, China responded by expanding restrictions on essential rare earth supplies. This put Western factories and defence production under immediate pressure. It forced the White House to de-escalate its tariff hikes and seek accommodation for a more predictable trade relationship.
Now, Washington is pressing ahead with targeted efforts to limit options for where Chinese companies sell, invest and operate. This includes restricting companies’ access to the US market beyond tariffs, while also curbing investment from China and increasingly banning the use of Chinese technology domestically. Despite China’s potent escalation options, the US is pursuing both stability and decoupling at the same time.
The lesson for Europeans is that talks and bargaining with Beijing can help contain escalation while enforcing their own rules across trade, investment and critical infrastructure.
How the EU navigates its season of decisions will determine whether it can successfully defend its industrial and security interests in the face of China’s threats of retaliation.
Three decisions for the EU
What China sells
Europe’s first decision is whether to accept a narrow trade settlement with China in October. Such a settlement—for example, focused on automotive exports, which the two sides are currently discussing—may ease some tensions. It could see China voluntarily limit the number of electric and hybrid vehicles it sends to the EU each year. Or it could involve expanding so-called “price undertakings” in which individual Chinese producers agree to market entry terms, such as minimum import prices, total volume limits or local investment commitments. Volkswagen Anhui, one of the German company’s China-based joint ventures, already agreed to such terms earlier this year.
However, this approach risks failing to address wider industrial challenges posed by the Chinese system. Sectors other than the car industry are already under pressure from China’s industrial policies, including batteries, wind equipment, robotics, machine tools, chemicals and biotechnologies. But a narrow agreement would leave these areas untouched.
Any deal the EU strikes must therefore address these particular issues and support a level of stability between the EU and China—while also preserving the bloc’s ability to tackle other distortions from China independently.
What the EU should do
Therefore, making a deal on one product cannot become a promise to tolerate distortions impacting on others. In the electric vehicle value chain, Brussels must retain its ability to launch anti-subsidy (and safeguard) investigations in other segments of the chain, like batteries, or sectors outside the scope of a settlement. The European Commission must also make use of the anti-circumvention tools it already has to close gaps created by Chinese producers redirecting exports through different locations or product categories. Unlike the Trump administration’s broad tariffs, trade defence measures calibrated to identified distortions would preserve competition in the single market while removing China’s artificial advantages.
The same logic must apply inside the single market, and Europe must maintain its autonomy to enforce a level playing field. This means the EU should be free to systematically launch and conclude investigations under the Foreign Subsidy Regulation across sectors where Chinese state financing is plausibly distorting competition in the single market. The bloc can also make assertive use of the international procurement instrument across every sector where documented procurement discrimination against European firms exists in China.
Furthermore, the EU must press ahead with upgrading its economic security toolbox, and make sure its contents are not beholden to any deal agreed with China. This includes developing a diversification instrument that could push firms in critical sectors to have a diversified supplier base (this could, for example, work by the EU placing tariffs on overdependent imports). It also means strengthening the anti-coercion instrument to lower the bar for activation, and adding a solidarity fund to compensate companies hit by retaliation and coercion.
Where China produces
Europe’s second decision is about what it expects in return when Chinese companies invest in the single market. Chinese investments in Europe (including Britain) have recovered from a previous lull, reaching almost €17bn in 2025 (nearly a quarter of all Chinese FDI), with 45% of that investment in the automotive and EV sector.
The problem for Europe is that, despite this rising investment, China’s exports are increasing at an even faster pace—supported by continued industrial policy support, persistently weak domestic demand and a weak yuan. Where Chinese investors are active in Europe, the risk persists that they will merely relocate final assembly while their supplier networks and technology remain tightly guarded. Without adequate safeguards, Chinese firms may set up “screwdriver factories” in the EU, which assemble largely pre-manufactured components, while retaining high-value activities in China. Indeed, Beijing has not only instructed its carmakers to follow this path, but also explicitly expanded its control levers to decide which automotive components are allowed for export.
What the EU should do
Europe’s trade and investment policies therefore have to work together. To ensure Chinese investors actually shift production to the continent, Europeans need to change the business arithmetic that makes exporting from China more profitable, whether by imposing tariffs or agreeing a managed trade deal. Where import barriers encourage Chinese investment, the EU must then ensure projects will develop local suppliers and support technology learning or transfer.
The EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, which is under negotiation, attempts to partially address this issue. Importantly, it marks a shift away from treating foreign investment in batteries, electric vehicles, solar power and critical raw materials as an automatic benefit. Under the plans, investments above €100m would have to meet four out of six conditions intended to generate industrial value in Europe (including introducing ownership limits, a joint venture condition, intellectual property sharing, local sourcing and more). Yet, as currently drafted, the only mandatory condition for foreign investors is to commit to local employment. The proposed design would create an à la carte system in which investors could avoid the requirements that are most important for supporting Europe’s industrial transition and scale-up.
It now falls to member states and the European Parliament to make more investment conditions mandatory if China wishes to enter Europe’s strategic industrial base. They should also future-proof the Industrial Accelerator Act by explicitly allowing the legislation to cover other sectors at the core of industrial competition, such as industrial robotics, wind equipment and medical technology.
What China controls
Europe’s third decision concerns where it allows Chinese suppliers a role in critical infrastructure and systems—and where they are excluded. Member states have in recent years strengthened their foreign investment screening powers and adopted a common approach to high-risk 5G suppliers. Yet the security risks today extend beyond these tools and sectors. They reach deep into European ports, energy systems and connected infrastructure.

By Professor Maurice Okoli, Ph.D*
This article was first published in Eurasia Review.
MOSCOW | 17 October 2026 (IDN) — Perhaps, BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), with the new members and partner states, summit in New Delhi, from 11 September to 13, produced a new round of significant declarations, adapting its collective policy toward an increasingly emerging architecture, while distinctively building an ‘Asian model’ of economic alliance. Under India’s chairmanship, the summit focused on building a reputation that has been developing for nearly two decades. The timing was, particularly, notable. The most important strategic message was coined: “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability.”
Addressing the BRICS summit of leading developing nations in New Delhi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi warned that rising geopolitical tensions could increasingly affect people worldwide and called for deepening cooperation and strengthening support across the Global South. “The number of conflicts and tensions in the world is continuously increasing, and this is having an increasingly negative and far-reaching impact on the lives of ordinary people,” Modi said, alongside leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. That was one of the main messages sent across the world. Founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, BRICS has expanded to 11 members representing about half the world’s population and a significant share of global economic output. It has sought greater representation for developing countries in global institutions and promoted alternative actions to Western-dominated financial systems. Pasted markdown
Geopolitics: Is BRICS Challenging the West?
BRICS leaders adopted the New Delhi Declaration, expressing deep concern about forging consensus on many strategic questions, backing greater use of local currencies in trade and stronger cross-border payment systems, and calling for cooperation on food security, energy, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, and climate action. The declaration was a significant breakthrough, but it also reflects competing positions on key regional and geopolitical issues, posing a complex diplomatic challenge amid ongoing conflicts and heightened geopolitical tensions. It emphasises collective support for a multipolar world order and operational and structural reforms at the United Nations, including its Security Council, as well as global financial institutions such as the World Bank (WB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The declaration showed that BRICS can move together and act on multilateral economic cooperation, and that this cooperation is sustainable in the Global South. This raises the question of whether India has used its presidency to push the BRICS grouping to become more capable of economic action, with reports indicating that India entered the role with more than just a diplomatic presence. For instance, during the financial year 2024-25, its total exports amounted to approximately $825 billion, with services accounting for an estimated $387 billion. Few developing countries can match New Delhi’s economic leverage, which stems from its large domestic market, expanding digital economy, and sustainable growth. Despite national preferences and differences among BRICS members, India is a major provider of digital public infrastructure, and its demography plays an increasingly important role in global consumption, production, and services. It therefore shows that BRICS members must build economic prosperity by opening doors. This new phase must strategically focus on broader economic leverage. Appropriately, India’s geography provides an additional layer of economic leverage, serving as a classic example for other Asian countries. Pasted markdown
Сorporate Economic Weight, Limited Collective Power
While BRICS’s economic weight is enormous, its ability to wield it collectively is not, some analysts argue. However, experts’ arguments closely connected to BRICS operational successes and achievements should not only be measured by whether it can pose an alternative to multinational institutions, but also whether it could make any noticeable difference, in terms of using its natural resources to increase regional trade, raise economic production and improve distribution across the Global South. Several experts portray BRICS as offering its member countries alternative pathways for channelling trade and investment that serve the collective interests of member countries–largely national development and poverty alleviation.
Meanwhile, scholars have reminded that BRICS emerged after the 2008 financial collapse and the failures of the World Trade Organization’s (WTO) Doha Round–trade negotiations aimed at reforming the international trading system in favour of Global South countries. Why would the BRICS want to take on the global governance responsibilities of the G7 members? This remains the central question among scholars today. However, many believe BRICS is more concerned with reforms and greater autonomy than with overthrowing the unravelling liberal international order. Pasted markdown
BRICS+ Financial Architecture
The group is noticeably dominated by China, which has the largest share of the group’s GDP, accounting for about 70% of the organisation’s total. The financial architecture of BRICS is made up of the New Development Bank (NDB) and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA). These components were signed into a treaty in 2014 and became active in 2015. The New Development Bank (NDB), formerly the BRICS Development Bank, is a multilateral development bank operated by the five BRICS states. Non-members can contribute to the NDB.
The bank primarily lends to infrastructure projects, with authorised lending of up to $34 billion annually. South Africa hosts the bank’s African headquarters. The bank started with $50 billion in capital, which grew to $100 billion over time. Records show Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa initially contributed $10 billion each, bringing the total to $50 billion. As of 2020, it had 53 projects underway worth around $15 billion. By 2025, the bank had approved more than $32 billion for 96 projects.
In 2021, Bangladesh, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and Uruguay joined the NDB during India’s 2026 presidency, which was estimated to be comprehensive and promising for BRICS, as India has outlined its framework of priorities, as it did during its G20 presidency several years ago. In close coordination with members and partner states within BRICS, India has balanced multifaceted interests and built mutual trust in the multipolar world system. The goal of transforming into a full-fledged international organisation must go beyond addressing current geopolitical challenges; it must also develop effective ways to engage in global development that reflect multipolarity. Today, BRICS collectively accounts for more than a quarter of the global economy and nearly half the world’s population. Pasted markdown
BRICS Advocates for Reforms at Financial Institutions
Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors of BRICS countries have called for reform of global developmental financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, seeking a stronger voice for emerging market economies. “We will continue to strengthen coordination among BRICS members to make international financial institutions more representative, transparent and accountable. With the growing share of emerging market and developing economies in global output and growth, reform of global economic governance remains a consistent BRICS priority,” Finance Chiefs of BRICS countries underlined in an official joint statement.
“We continue to have serious concerns with the unilateral imposition of trade and finance-related actions, including the raising of tariffs and non-tariff measures, which distort trade and are inconsistent with World Trade Organisation rules,” the statement said. “We encourage the BRICS Payment Task Force to continue discussions, building on the ongoing work, to facilitate practical solutions for cross-border payments among BRICS countries, which are fast, low-cost, more accessible, efficient, transparent, and safe,” the statement said. While acknowledging the work of the BRICS payment task force, the finance chiefs pushed for greater interoperability of payment systems across member nations. It also noted that India will push for progress on linking digital currencies across BRICS countries. Pasted markdown
BRICS-Africa Transitioning from Diplomacy to Strategic Economy
South Africa (2010), Ethiopia, and Egypt (2024), as fully-fledged BRICS members, seem to be shifting from a policy of strategic ambiguity to a kind of assertive flexibility. South Africa, Ethiopia and Egypt are also positioning themselves as leading African voices for the Global South while, at the same time, maintaining relationships with competing Western powers. In principle, Africa generally collaborates with the United States and Asia-Pacific partners while, to a certain degree, striking multifaceted ties with Russia, and operates within the framework of the BRICS domain.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, and President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi of the Arab Republic of Egypt held separate conversations on the current status and prospects for their relations, and further discussed ways of strengthening BRICS strategic partnership in politics and security, economics and finance, and cultural and humanitarian ties, while exchanging divergent views on current international and regional issues that are of common significance to global development. South Africa, Ethiopia and Egypt, however, plan to take new initiatives to improve and strengthen relations within BRICS.
