Egypt is seeking to expand trade with Thailand and attract Thai investment in manufacturing, food industries, textiles, and tourism, Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said at an Egyptian-Thai business forum in Bangkok on Friday.
Organized by the Federation of Thai Industries in cooperation with the Thai-Egyptian Business Council, the forum is part of the Egyptian FM's agenda during his visit to Thailand. It also marks the third session of the countries’ joint ministerial committee.
In his address, Abdelatty stressed the Egyptian government’s commitment to opening new avenues for trade and investment and fostering partnerships between Egyptian and Thai private-sector companies.
He highlighted Egypt’s large domestic market, developing infrastructure, and strategic location, as well as investment opportunities in the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZone). He also pointed to Egypt’s free trade agreements, which provide preferential access to regional markets, including the African Continental Free Trade Area.
The Egyptian FM urged Thai companies to explore opportunities in manufacturing, food processing, textiles, rubber, tourism, and logistics.
Moreover, Abdelatty met with Pimjai Lee Isarankul, president of the Federation of Thai Industries, on the sidelines of the forum to discuss expanding industrial cooperation and joint investment.
The talks also covered closer engagement between the Thai federation and the Federation of Egyptian Industries, exchanges of business delegations, and participation in specialized trade fairs.
Abdelatty stressed the need to translate identified opportunities into concrete projects that benefit both countries.
In a separate meeting with Daivon Lertsonrang, chief executive of the Export-Import Bank of Thailand, the Egyptian FM discussed financing arrangements to support bilateral trade and investment.
He also highlighted the importance of using the bank’s financing, insurance, and investment-guarantee tools to encourage Thai companies to expand their operations in Egypt.
Furthermore, Abdelatty outlined Egypt’s potential as a regional manufacturing and export hub, citing opportunities in the SCZone and access to African, Arab, and European markets through free trade agreements.
He also addressed expanding credit facilities and facilitating payments to support exporters and importers.
In conclusion, the Egyptian FM reviewed the outcomes of the Alamein-Africa Business Forum with Lertsonrang and called for financing to support Egyptian-Thai partnerships in Africa.
Foreign ministry spokesman Ambassador Nader Zaki said on Saturday that effective diplomacy adds value to Egypt’s international presence and the national economy, MENA reported.
Zaki added that Egypt’s diplomatic activity concerns the nature of its role, not simply its geographical reach.
His remarks followed Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty’s visit to Bangkok to participate in the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group, held from 12 to 18 October.
During the visit, Abdelatty held bilateral talks with senior officials and joined multilateral meetings on geopolitical crises and their repercussions for the global economy.

articles.summary: UNCTAD backs export diversification in Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone  Fibre2Fashion
articles.full_text:
17 Oct 26
Insights
- UNCTAD has set out a project for Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone to diversify exports, build regional value and supply chains, and expand SME participation in AfCFTA markets.
- Diagnostics, policy dialogues and digital tools will identify priority industries and export opportunities, improve SME access to finance and technology, and target women-led SMEs and gender parity.
The project places particular emphasis on strengthening productive capacities, helping SMEs access finance and digital technologies, and supporting women-led SMEs. The wider Mano River Union (MRU) region comprises Côte d’Ivoire, Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
The MRU region faces structural constraints including limited economic diversification, low levels of industrialisation, significant gender inequalities and vulnerability to external economic shocks. Intra-regional trade remains limited, largely informal and concentrated in low value-added products, limiting opportunities for productive transformation and job creation, UNCTAD said in a press release.
At the same time, the region has considerable potential through abundant natural resources, strong agricultural prospects and a growing young population. Effective AfCFTA implementation could help the countries build on these strengths by diversifying exports, strengthening regional value chains and increasing SME participation in regional markets.
The project will conduct national diagnostic studies and sector-specific assessments to identify export diversification opportunities, priority industries and constraints to SME participation in regional value chains. National consultations, regional policy dialogues and capacity-building workshops will aim to strengthen public and private stakeholders’ ability to assess trade and industrial development opportunities, improve policy coordination and support the implementation of AfCFTA commitments.
Other activities include peer learning on SME financing, digitalisation and regional value chains, as well as the development and enhancement of digital tools for trade data collection, market intelligence and identifying export opportunities. The work will be complemented by assessments of digital and financing solutions and targeted capacity-building for policymakers and SMEs.
Expected outcomes include stronger institutional and policy capacities for export diversification and inclusive industrial development; better SME access to digital technologies, market information and finance; stronger regional partnerships for value-added cross-border trade and regional industrial clusters; deeper regional economic integration; increased capacity among women-led SMEs and underserved economic actors; and more diversified, competitive and resilient economies in the MRU region.
On gender equality and women’s economic empowerment, the project will address barriers faced by women in informal trade and small-scale business, particularly in accessing finance, digital technologies and regional market opportunities. It aims to strengthen women’s participation in regional trade and ensure they benefit from export diversification and more inclusive financing opportunities. The project is classified as GEN II under the African Development Bank (AfDB) Gender Marker System.
Gender will be mainstreamed across the project through national consultations that identify gender gaps and opportunities in regional value chains and export diversification, with both women and men consulted and their experiences reflected in studies, assessments and validation workshops. A country gap assessment will examine how small-scale traders, women-owned and women-led businesses and young entrepreneurs use digital technologies along potential supply chains, while a cross-border trade mobile application will include options to collect and analyse sex-disaggregated data.
AfCFTA workshops will include an agenda on the operationalisation of the Women and Youth Protocol. Links with the AfDB’s Affirmative Finance Action for Women in Africa initiative and opportunities to access climate finance will be explored for women-led SMEs. Two regional reports will assess how leveraging the MRU’s export potential can promote gender equality and environmental sustainability, and women’s associations will participate in the regional stakeholder workshop.
The project will aim for gender parity across its activities, with a target of 50 per cent women and 50 per cent men. Sex-disaggregated data will be collected throughout implementation to monitor participation and results.
UNCTAD said the project supports the MRU’s regional integration and economic development priorities, the African Union’s Agenda 2063 and AfCFTA implementation. It also contributes directly to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) covering no poverty; gender equality; decent work and economic growth; industry, innovation and infrastructure; reduced inequalities; responsible consumption and production; climate action; peace, justice and strong institutions; and partnerships for the goals.

Narayan said the amount was not tied to a fixed investment timetable and would depend on the outcome of bids.
"We are prepared to invest between $3 billion and $5 billion (in India)," he told a select group of journalists.
DP World, which has built an integrated Indian network spanning ports, rail and inland logistics, is seeking to expand its footprint as the world's most populous country looks to strengthen domestic connectivity and become a larger manufacturing and export hub.
The company announced an additional $5 billion India investment commitment in October 2025, over and above $3 billion invested in the country over three decades.
India's infrastructure push has delivered substantial improvements, Narayan said, but port and rail development and the processes governing project execution need to move faster.
"One always hopes things could happen faster," he said, pointing to the long wait for the Vadhavan project and arguing that infrastructure development should keep pace with progress in roads, airports and power.
DP World is prepared to bid for new opportunities, expand its rail network and increase port capacity, Narayan said. The company currently operates six port concessions in India and plans to increase its railheads from eight to 12, according to him.
India's growing economic scale makes it attractive despite historically weaker returns on invested capital, Narayan said. Currency depreciation, driven in part by the country's energy import bill, has weighed on returns, while infrastructure upgrades, digitisation and the shift towards renewable energy could improve the outlook.
The proposed investment would also help strengthen DP World's wider supply-chain network, rather than simply expand its Indian business, he said.
The investment push comes as disruptions around key West Asian maritime chokepoints force shipping companies to reroute cargo, add capacity and absorb higher operating costs.
Narayan said DP World's flagship Jebel Ali port in Dubai, which normally handles about 15 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) annually, was facing a severe reduction in activity because of restricted access. He said the disruption was affecting cargo flows well beyond the Gulf, creating congestion at ports and logistics facilities across parts of Asia and Africa.
The impact extends beyond the port itself, he said, because Jebel Ali serves as a major transshipment hub linking Asian manufacturing centres with markets in the Middle East, Africa and Europe.
DP World had expected Jebel Ali's port operations to generate about $1.2 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA), but Narayan said the disruption would materially reduce the group's earnings outlook. He estimated that global EBITDA could fall to about $5.8 billion from a level of roughly $6.2 billion to $6.4 billion, with growth elsewhere cushioning part of the lost contribution.
The company is exploring alternative routes through other Gulf ports and overland connections, including routes through Saudi Arabia, Narayan said. But building replacement capacity takes time, and he estimated that new port capacity could take two to three years to develop.
"Port capacity is not created overnight," he said, warning that the full consequences of the disruption may take time to emerge.
The crisis also underscores the growing cost of building redundancy into supply chains. Companies that once prioritised lean inventories, low costs and just-in-time deliveries are increasingly seeking alternative suppliers, routes and production centres to reduce their exposure to geopolitical shocks.
Narayan said global trade now required substantially more shipping capacity to move less cargo than before, as longer routes and operational inefficiencies absorbed available capacity. Higher interest rates, fuel expenses and other operating costs were adding to the burden.
"Who do you think pays for all this disruption? You - as a consumer," he said, arguing that the additional costs would ultimately be passed through to buyers of goods.
He expects shorter supply chains and a greater emphasis on regional production to reshape trade flows over time, potentially increasing the importance of north-south trade between Asia, Africa and other emerging markets.
For India, the opportunity lies in expanding manufacturing and exports while building the port, rail and inland logistics infrastructure needed to connect producers with global markets.
Narayan said India's exports and imports currently account for a relatively small share of its overall economy, leaving considerable room for growth. A substantial increase in trade would require a corresponding expansion in logistics capacity, he said.
However, he cautioned that resilience would come at a cost. Maintaining alternative routes, suppliers and inventory buffers would make supply chains more expensive and capital-intensive than the lean systems businesses had previously pursued.
"The world has to come to peace," Narayan said, arguing that physical infrastructure alone cannot eliminate the risks posed by conflict.

The 11th Annual London Political Summit and Awards (LPSA) 2026 continued its celebration of outstanding leadership with the presentation of awards to distinguished traditional rulers, business executives, entrepreneurs, professionals and community champions whose contributions span economic development, public service, education, diplomacy and community advancement.

Gambian High Commissioner Named Commonwealth Diplomat of the Year 2026
A major highlight of the evening was the presentation of the LPSA Commonwealth Diplomat of the Year 2026 Award to Her Excellency Dr. Fatou Bensouda, High Commissioner of The Gambia to the United Kingdom.

The honour recognised the High Commissioner’s diplomatic engagement and contributions associated with peace, justice, equality, international cooperation and constructive international relations.
Her recognition also highlighted the importance of diplomacy in strengthening Commonwealth ties, facilitating trade and investment, and fostering mutual understanding among nations.
Awards of Appreciation to Partners and Community Champions
The formal recognition segment concluded with awards of appreciation to selected dignitaries, partners and community champions whose support has contributed to the Summit’s activities and wider objectives.
Recipients included HRH Oba Ambassador Dr. Olusegun Aderemi JP; HRM Obonganwan Marie Erete; Chief Dr. Clifford Atile; Alhaji Musa M. Jazuli; Mr. Juan Cabrera; Kachi Okezie Esq.; Heritage TV; Voice Magazine; The Nigeria Voice; and other supporters.
The awards acknowledged the value of collective effort in delivering international engagements that bring together political institutions, diplomatic missions, business communities and civil society.
The organisers also expressed appreciation to participating governments, parliamentary hosts, diplomatic representatives, sponsors, partner organisations and individual supporters whose contributions helped make the 2026 programme possible.

Beyond the award presentations, the 11th London Political Summit and Awards reaffirmed its broader commitment to Pan-Africanism, democratic governance, peacebuilding and sustainable economic development.

Its advocacy for “Trade for Peace” reflects the principle that constructive commercial relationships can create shared interests, strengthen diplomatic engagement, encourage dialogue and foster cooperation between countries and communities.
The programme also highlighted environmental protection and climate resilience as important considerations in development planning, alongside investment, institutional accountability and responsible leadership.
The tribute to the late Rt. Hon. Raila Amolo Odinga gave these discussions added significance. His longstanding commitment to democratic reform, political dialogue and reconciliation remains an important reference point for leaders seeking peaceful solutions to political differences and stronger democratic institutions.
In this regard, LPSA 2026 served both as a commemoration of an influential African statesman and as a renewed call for practical leadership, stronger partnerships and sustained action towards peace and development.

Oliver Ryan MP; Mr. Joel Popoola of the IoD Africa Group; Mr. Juan Cabrera of the IoD Natural Resources Group; Ms. Julie Ojiambo; gala host Ms. Rosé Graham; participating diplomatic missions; government delegations from Nigeria and other African countries; traditional rulers; business leaders; community champions; and all those who contributed to the three-day programme.

Looking ahead, he disclosed that the proposed 12th Annual London Political Summit and Awards in 2027 could be complemented by an African edition in Kenya, subject to further consultations, planning and confirmation with relevant partners and stakeholders.
If realised, the initiative would extend the Summit’s engagement beyond London, creating further opportunities to connect African political institutions, diplomatic communities, businesses and development partners.

articles.title: Egypt’s Economy Shows Signs of Improvement as Structural Reforms Advance, Says Planning Min. - Sada Elbalad English
articles.summary: Egypt’s Economy Shows Signs of Improvement as Structural Reforms Advance, Says Planning Min.  Sada Elbalad English
articles.full_text:
Egypt’s economy is showing signs of improvement following the implementation of structural reforms and measures aimed at strengthening macroeconomic stability, Planning and Economic Development Minister Ahmed Rostom said, as the government advances its National Economic Transformation Programme to boost investment, production and sustainable growth.
Speaking at the conclusion of his participation in the 81st Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group in Bangkok, Thailand, Rostom highlighted improvements in Egypt’s economic indicators toward the end of the previous fiscal year, attributing the progress to a series of structural and cross-sectoral reforms designed to mitigate the effects of geopolitical tensions and international economic uncertainty.
The minister’s participation included high-level meetings with international financial institutions, regional development banks, government officials and global investment funds, with discussions focusing on expanding investment cooperation, mobilizing development finance and supporting Egypt’s economic priorities.
National Transformation Programme Targets Sustainable Growth
Rostom said the Egyptian government is working across state institutions to implement its National Economic Transformation Programme, which aims to consolidate macroeconomic stability and shift the economy toward a growth model driven by higher production and investment.
The programme is also intended to ensure that the benefits of economic development translate more directly into improvements in living standards, while establishing a sustainable framework for growth over the coming years.
The government’s approach places greater emphasis on productive economic activity and investment-led expansion, amid continued challenges stemming from regional instability and global economic pressures.
World Bank Partnership to Support Infrastructure Financing
Innovative financing mechanisms featured prominently in the minister’s discussions, particularly the development of an infrastructure project financing guarantee mechanism in partnership with the World Bank Group.
According to Rostom, the proposed mechanism is designed to reduce investment risks for private-sector participants, mobilize additional capital and provide access to long-term financing in local currency.
The initiative is expected to support nationally prioritized projects across several sectors, including water sustainability, renewable energy, green transport and industrial infrastructure.
By attracting private investment and expanding financing options, the mechanism is intended to improve public spending efficiency while easing financing pressures on the state budget.
The initiative reflects Egypt’s broader efforts to develop financing structures capable of supporting infrastructure investment without relying exclusively on conventional public expenditure.
High-Level Meetings Focus on Investment and Development Finance
During the meetings in Bangkok, Rostom held discussions with senior officials from major international and regional financial institutions.
Among those he met were World Bank Group President Ajay Banga; International Finance Corporation (IFC) Managing Director Makhtar Diop; and World Bank Vice President for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, Ousmane Dione.
He also met African Development Bank Group President Sidi Ould Tah, Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA) President Abdullah Al-Musabeeh, and International Islamic Trade Finance Corporation (ITFC) Chief Executive Officer Adeeb Al-Aama.
Additional discussions involved government representatives, including Canada’s minister responsible for international development, Jordan’s minister of planning and international cooperation, and Kuwait’s finance minister.
Meetings with representatives of sovereign and independent investment funds in Sweden and Norway, as well as officials from the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), focused on strengthening cooperation and expanding foreign investment opportunities in Egypt.
Food Security and Global Economic Risks on the Agenda
The minister also participated in broader discussions on global economic challenges, including disruptions to food security arising from tensions affecting strategically important maritime corridors.
Such disruptions have raised concerns about the reliability of international supply chains and the costs associated with transporting essential commodities.
The discussions underscored the importance of international cooperation and financing arrangements capable of helping economies manage external shocks and strengthen their resilience.
Human Capital and Technology Key to Economic Transformation
Rostom highlighted Egypt’s focus on human capital development and skills investment, emphasizing the need to align education and training outcomes with labor-market requirements.
He also pointed to the growing importance of artificial intelligence and modern technologies in preparing a workforce capable of supporting the digital transformation of the Egyptian economy.
Linking skills development to the needs of businesses and emerging industries is a key element of the government’s stated ambition to strengthen productivity and support a more investment-driven economic model.
Regional Integration Seen as a Growth Opportunity
Concluding his participation, Rostom reaffirmed the importance of Egypt’s cooperation with international financial institutions and regional development banks in mobilizing funding and technical expertise for development priorities.
He also called for greater activation of continental and regional free trade agreements to facilitate capital flows and develop integrated regional value chains.
Stronger regional economic links, he said, could help improve the competitiveness of participating economies in global markets.
As Egypt pursues its National Economic Transformation Programme, the government’s priorities include sustaining macroeconomic stability, attracting private investment, expanding productive capacity and improving the alignment between economic development and citizens’ living standards.

South African Prez cites historic ties, seeks stronger India cooperation
The South African president said the two countries' partnership now encompassed trade, investment, technology, education and international cooperation
Listen to This Article
India and South Africa are 'bound together' by deep historical ties and common democratic values, President Cyril Ramaphosa has said while inaugurating a major expansion of a zinc mine operated by an Indian conglomerate in the Northern Cape province.
Ramaphosa made the remarks on Friday at the inauguration of Vedanta's Gamsberg Phase II concentrator plant in Aggeneys, in the presence of Indian High Commissioner Prabhat Kumar and Consul General Ruby Jaspreet, among other dignitaries.
A concentrator plant separates valuable minerals from mined ore to produce a more concentrated material for further processing. At the Gamsberg plant, the zinc concentrate can be processed further to produce refined zinc metal.
The Consulate General of India in Cape Town said in a post on X on Saturday that the Phase II expansion involved an investment of approximately ZAR 10 billion (around Rs 5,757 crore), making it one of South Africa's largest mining investments of the past decade.
"This occasion is also an important affirmation of the enduring relationship between South Africa and India," Ramaphosa said during the inauguration event, according to an official statement.
Also Read
"Our two countries are bound together by deep historical ties, common democratic values and a shared commitment to development," he said.
The South African president said the two countries' partnership now encompassed trade, investment, technology, education and international cooperation, adding that the relationship had grown from a shared struggle against colonialism and oppression.
"Today, more than 150 Indian companies have established a presence in South Africa, contributing investment, employment and industrial expertise," Ramaphosa said, describing Vedanta as an important example of the bilateral partnership.
Ramaphosa said he had engaged Indian business leaders on expanding trade and investment during the 18th BRICS Summit. Discussions covered manufacturing, energy, infrastructure, technology and mineral processing.
India and South Africa are both members of BRICS, an intergovernmental grouping that promotes cooperation among emerging and developing economies on trade, investment, development finance and global governance. The grouping's 18th summit was held in New Delhi last month.
Ramaphosa on Friday urged investors to create local employment, develop industries, transfer skills and contribute to surrounding communities, saying sustainable investment should generate benefits beyond returns for shareholders.
He also welcomed Vedanta's plans to establish zinc-smelting capacity in Northern Cape, South Africa's largest province. He said this would help the country move further along the value chain, from producing zinc concentrate to refined metal.
Vedanta, an Indian conglomerate, acquired the Gamsberg asset from Anglo American in 2011, and Ramaphosa inaugurated the mine's first phase in February 2019. Vedanta Zinc International manages the group's zinc assets in South Africa and Namibia.
The Phase II expansion will double Gamsberg's annual ore-processing capacity from four million tonnes to eight million tonnes and increase its annual zinc-in-concentrate production capacity to approximately 500,000 tonnes, according to the company's website.

articles.title: The only country in the world that operates a floating nuclear facility wants to bring it to Africa, with its largest African partner in focus - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: The only country in the world that operates a floating nuclear facility wants to bring it to Africa, with its largest African partner in focus  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Russia is actively engaging African nations regarding the deployment of its floating nuclear power technology.
- Guinea and Russia initiated collaboration talks on such projects in 2024, signing a memorandum of understanding at SPIEF.
- Russia's floating nuclear power plant, the Akademik Lomonosov, offers mobile energy solutions and can provide electricity, heat, and desalinated water to remote areas.
- Egypt is currently a primary focus for Russia's expansion in Africa, using the technology to grow its nuclear sector and foster local shipbuilding.
This conversation took center stage back in 2024, when the Kremlin and the Republic of Guinea began assessing the feasibility of collaborating on a floating nuclear project.
At the time, the two countries signed a memorandum of understanding at the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum (SPIEF) to this effect.
Afterwards, a statement from Rosatom, Russia’s state-owned nuclear company, read, "A floating nuclear power plant is a site with one or more nuclear reactors, located on a platform at sea.
It is an autonomous site that can provide electricity and heat to areas with difficult access, such as the cold Northern territories. It can also provide drinking water to dry areas via desalination techniques."
The statement further detailed, "The parties will study the possibility of implementing the floating power units project in the Republic of Guinea within the framework of the agreement reached and will work out the terms and conditions of the project."
Currently, Russia is the only country in the world that has a floating nuclear facility.
The country operates the Akademik Lomonosov, the world's first operational floating nuclear power plant.
It is essentially a nuclear power station built onto a ship-like platform that can supply electricity and heat to remote coastal communities.
Unlike a conventional nuclear power station, it can be stationed in a remote port rather than requiring a large land-based site.
Very recently, according to Rosatom’s nuclear chief, Alexey Likhachev, the company reiterated its intent to bring its floating nuclear power to Africa.
He noted that this time, Egypt is a region of interest, given the North African country’s intent to expand its nuclear capabilities.
Egypt aims to use the technology to facilitate localized shipbuilding and expand cooperation into small nuclear power plants.
As seen on Sputnik, Alexey Likhachev made this known to reporters he spoke to on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week.
The Rosatom chief further revealed that the initiative is not exclusive to Egypt, as other African countries that have already established a nuclear framework with Moscow are also in the mix for its floating nuclear technology.
As of 2025, official data showed that around 15 African countries had nuclear cooperation with Russia, including some of the continent’s largest economies.
Countries such as Morocco, Egypt, Nigeria, Ghana, Ethiopia, and Tanzania not only have nuclear cooperation with Russia but also boast a military partnership with the Eurasian giant.
Of these countries, Egypt is currently Russia’s top partner in Africa.
Partnership between Egypt and Russia
In August 2025, Russia officially listed Egypt as its largest African trade and economic partner, underscoring the two countries' expanding relationship.
According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, bilateral trade topped $9 billion in 2024, highlighting Egypt's vital position in Moscow's engagement on the continent.
The statement came as Moscow and Cairo celebrated 82 years of diplomatic relations, which have historically included political, military, and economic cooperation.
At the core of their relationship is Egypt's first nuclear power station, El-Dabaa, which Russia's state-owned Rosatom is now building.
Launched in 2022, the project represents a long-term investment by both nations in their alliance.
The facility is intended to increase Egypt's electricity-generating capacity, diversify its energy mix, and strengthen Russia's position as a significant stakeholder in Egypt's infrastructure development.

With a proposed deep seaport, a renewed push for a $10bn liquefied natural gas project, more than 1,600 kilometres of roads and a cargo airport, Ogun State is pursuing an ambitious transformation into a major industrial, maritime and logistics hub.
Ogun State is seeking to redefine its economic identity, leveraging its strategic location, expanding infrastructure and established manufacturing base to attract more than $17 billion in potential investments that could reshape its industrial landscape.
At the centre of the ambition are two major initiatives: a proposed deep seaport and special economic zone backed by global logistics company DP World, with an initial investment of more than $7 billion, and renewed efforts to advance the long-delayed OgunLNG project, for which the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) has proposed an initial investment of $10 billion.
Together, the projects offer a vision of Ogun as more than a state benefiting from its proximity to Lagos. They present the prospect of an economy with stronger maritime connections, expanded energy infrastructure, new industrial clusters and greater capacity to participate in domestic and international trade.
The scale of the proposed investments reflects Governor Dapo Abiodun’s broader economic strategy, which has prioritised infrastructure development, private-sector partnerships and an enabling environment for businesses since he assumed office on May 29, 2019.
However, the proposed $17 billion-plus investment pipeline should not be mistaken for funds already committed and deployed. The projects remain at different stages of development, and their eventual impact will depend on financing, regulatory approvals, construction and successful implementation.
Even so, the initiatives underscore the administration’s ambition to turn Ogun’s geographical advantages and growing infrastructure network into a platform for sustained industrial growth.
Infrastructure lays the groundwork
For Ogun, the drive towards industrial expansion begins with infrastructure.
The state government says it has constructed and rehabilitated more than 1,600 kilometres of roads since 2019, connecting communities, industrial centres, agricultural areas and commercial districts across its 20 local government areas.
The investment is intended to address a fundamental requirement of economic development: the ability to move people, raw materials and finished products efficiently.
For manufacturers, improved road networks can reduce transportation costs, ease access to suppliers and markets, and strengthen distribution systems. Farmers and agro-processors also stand to benefit from improved connections between production areas and commercial outlets.
Ogun’s proximity to Lagos, Nigeria’s commercial nerve centre, gives it a natural advantage. But the state’s longer-term competitiveness depends on how effectively it complements that location with reliable transport infrastructure and an environment in which businesses can expand.
Rail connectivity through the Lagos-Ibadan standard-gauge railway provides another transportation option, while road projects, including the rehabilitation of the Sagamu-Ijebu-Ode-Ore Road, are intended to improve access to markets and strengthen economic links, particularly in Ogun East.
The proposed benefits of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway could further improve regional connectivity as the project progresses.
Aviation infrastructure is also part of the strategy. The Gateway Agro-Cargo International Airport at Iperu-Remo, developed during Abiodun’s first term and subsequently commissioned for operations, is intended to facilitate cargo transportation, agricultural exports and logistics.
The airport could provide an additional channel for businesses requiring faster access to domestic and international markets, complementing the state’s road and rail networks.
In June 2025, Abiodun outlined his ambition to make Ogun the most connected subnational entity in Nigeria through an integrated network of road, rail, air and water transportation.
The underlying objective is to ensure that infrastructure serves as an engine of economic activity rather than an end in itself. For the administration, better connectivity is expected to strengthen industrial competitiveness, attract private capital and create the conditions for large-scale investment.
DP World agreement puts Ogun’s coastline in focus
Ogun’s maritime ambitions received a major boost on September 24, 2026, when the state government signed memoranda of understanding with DP World MEA FZE in Paris, France, for the proposed development of the Gateway Deep Sea Port and the Ogun State Blue Marine Special Economic Zone.
President Bola Tinubu witnessed the signing, underscoring the national significance attached to the proposed development.
With an initial investment of more than $7 billion, the project is intended to establish Ogun as a stronger player in maritime trade, shipping, logistics and industrial production.
The proposed Blue Marine Special Economic Zone is expected to cover more than 10,000 hectares, providing space for manufacturing facilities, warehouses, logistics operators and other businesses seeking to operate close to port infrastructure.
The development is projected to generate more than 50,000 direct jobs, although the actual employment impact will depend on the project's implementation, the pace of construction and the number of businesses that eventually establish operations within the zone.
The potential benefits extend beyond the port itself. International shipping facilities can attract freight forwarders, transport companies, distribution businesses, exporters and manufacturers, creating opportunities for a broader network of commercial activities.
For Ogun, the combination of a deep seaport and a special economic zone could help connect the state’s manufacturing base directly to international markets, improve the movement of imported raw materials and finished goods, and encourage new industrial investments.
The proposed zone could also attract businesses involved in processing, assembly, storage and distribution, potentially creating an industrial ecosystem around the maritime facility.
According to the state government's proposed timeline, construction is expected to commence in November 2026 following groundbreaking, with substantial completion projected within approximately two and a half years. The schedule remains subject to implementation arrangements and progress.
If realised as envisaged, the project could significantly alter the economic importance of Ogun’s Atlantic coastline, giving the state a more prominent role in Nigeria’s maritime and logistics value chain.
OgunLNG revival adds an energy dimension
While the proposed seaport has brought renewed attention to Ogun’s coastal development prospects, the renewed push for the OgunLNG project introduces another important dimension: energy.
During discussions with NNPC representatives at Iperu in Ikenne Local Government Area, Abiodun disclosed a proposed initial investment of $10 billion by the national oil company in the long-delayed liquefied natural gas project associated with the Olokola coastal corridor.
The renewed engagement has revived interest in a project whose development has faced years of delay, raising the possibility of fresh investment in gas infrastructure and related industrial activities.
NNPC was represented at the meeting by its Chief Financial Officer, Adedapo Segun, on behalf of the Group Chief Executive Officer, Bayo Ojulari.
Discussions around the project have highlighted the requirement for approximately 1,728 hectares of land and about 2.5 kilometres of Atlantic coastline. The Ogun State Government has indicated its willingness to facilitate land arrangements and consider relevant incentives to advance the initiative.
OgunLNG remains a proposed investment under active discussions. Its realisation will depend on further agreements and the completion of the necessary implementation processes.
Nevertheless, the renewed engagement highlights the importance of energy infrastructure to Ogun’s industrial ambitions. Manufacturing, processing and other energy-intensive industries require dependable energy supplies to operate efficiently, control production costs and compete in wider markets.
A major gas development could also create opportunities in engineering, construction, equipment supply, transportation, maintenance and other supporting services.
If delivered, OgunLNG could complement the proposed seaport and special economic zone, potentially strengthening the case for locating new industrial facilities along the coast.
The relationship between the projects is particularly significant. The port could facilitate international trade, the special economic zone could accommodate industrial and logistics businesses, while energy infrastructure could support productive activities requiring reliable gas supplies.

articles.title: US eases travel warning for Tanzania as Americans lead visitor market in its $4.4 billion tourism industry - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: US eases travel warning for Tanzania as Americans lead visitor market in its $4.4 billion tourism industry  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- The United States lowered Tanzania’s nationwide travel advisory on 16 October.
- Americans are now advised to exercise increased caution rather than reconsider travel.
- The change matters to a tourism industry that earned $4.41 billion in 2025.
- Stricter advice remains for the Mtwara border area adjoining Mozambique.
The decision comes as the United States remains Tanzania’s leading visitor source market, giving Washington’s assessment particular relevance to safari operators, hotels and other tourism businesses.
Tanzania welcomed approximately 2.29 million international tourists in 2025, up from 2.14 million a year earlier. Tourism earnings increased by 13%, outpacing the growth in arrivals as visitor spending also rose.
The advisory change follows nearly a year of heightened caution after Tanzania’s disputed 2025 election, when American officials warned of protests and potential travel disruptions.
According to the US State Department’s updated advisory, issued on 16 October 2026, Tanzania has moved from Level 3, “Reconsider Travel”, to Level 2, “Exercise Increased Caution”. Its published history confirms the decrease.
Why the American market matters
The latest official International Visitors’ Exit Survey, compiled by Tanzanian institutions including the central bank and statistics bureau, identifies the United States, Italy and France as the country’s leading source markets.
The survey puts annual tourism receipts at $4.41 billion in 2025, compared with $3.90 billion in 2024. Average visitor spending reached $289 per person per night.
Tanzania’s attractions include the Serengeti, Ngorongoro, Mount Kilimanjaro and Zanzibar. The sector connects wildlife and beach tourism with accommodation, transport, guiding and other services, making international visitor confidence commercially important.
The downgrade could support that confidence, although there is no evidence yet that it has increased bookings or revenue.
Warnings remain near Mozambique
Washington retains Level 3 advice for the Mtwara border area adjoining Mozambique, including the A19 highway, citing terrorism risks. US government employees require special authorisation to travel there.
The revised nationwide advisory also adds a health risk indicator, noting limited medical services, particularly outside Dar es Salaam and Arusha. Other cautions include crime, unrest, arbitrary enforcement of laws and the targeting of gay and lesbian people.
The department has not specified the assessment behind the downgrade. Travellers are still advised to avoid demonstrations and arrange insurance covering medical evacuation.
